question: In women on continuous CTG monitoring in labour, what proportion of hourly fetal heart rate assessments had an in-person 'fresh eyes' review by a second clinician documented before the next hourly assessment?
why: Delayed or absent fresh-eyes review of the CTG is a recurring theme in avoidable intrapartum stillbirth and brain injury cases; the corpus holds general intrapartum care and PPH audits [1] but no closed-loop audit of fresh-eyes CTG review timing.

standard.source: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.3.6 (2022)
standard.wording: Obtain an in-person review of every hourly assessment (see recommendation 1.3.5) by another clinician ("fresh eyes") for women on CTG, to be completed before the next assessment takes place.

pass: The hourly CTG assessment has a documented fresh-eyes review (name/role and time) by a second clinician, completed before the next hourly assessment is due
population: Inclusion: all women on continuous CTG monitoring in established labour. Exclusion: births before continuous CTG was started, home births.
sample: 40 consecutive women on continuous CTG monitoring in labour over the last 4 weeks, one CTG episode of at least 3 hours per woman
data_source: Labour ward CTG trace annotations and electronic partogram/labour record

template.note: number of hourly CTG assessments during the labour reviewed
how many had a documented second-clinician review before the next assessment

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a timed 'fresh eyes review due at __:__' prompt to the CTG trace and electronic labour record that is generated automatically at each hourly assessment and must be signed by a second clinician before it can be marked complete.
reaudit: At 12 weeks after the prompt is introduced, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward forum and maternity governance meeting; if compliance improves, embed the CTG fresh-eyes prompt as a fixed field in the electronic labour record build
evidence: [1892] intrapartum care and PPH: before → after (proforma change)
no closed-loop audit of fresh-eyes CTG review timing found in the library
pitfalls: Paper CTG annotations are often illegible or missing a time → agree a single place (trace margin or e-record) and a minimum data set with the labour ward before cycle 1
Small numbers if the unit has few continuous-CTG labours in the sample window → extend the collection period rather than lowering the sample
Staff may see the fresh-eyes prompt as another tick-box → involve labour ward coordinators in designing the prompt and explain the Each Baby Counts rationale
Definition of 'in-person' review may be interpreted loosely (a verbal comment vs a documented review) → fix the definition and a single documentation location before data collection starts
Gains fade once the audit team rotates → make the fresh-eyes field mandatory in the EPR build rather than relying on a poster reminder
pearls: Recruit a labour ward co-ordinator and a supervisor of midwives/PMA as co-investigators so the change has authority on the ward
Agree the exact fresh-eyes documentation field and audit definition with labour ward before cycle 1 starts
Time the audit to include day and night shifts, as fresh-eyes reviews are more often missed at night
Share individual near-miss examples (anonymised) at the labour ward forum to build buy-in before the second cycle
Keep the re-audit sample the same size and season to allow fair comparison
effort: ~30 min per 10 labours from the CTG trace and electronic labour record

question: In women with a low risk of complications having intermittent auscultation in established first stage of labour, what proportion of documented auscultations were performed at least once every 15 minutes?
why: RCEM's Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK reviews repeatedly identify failure to follow the recommended frequency and technique of intermittent auscultation as a contributory factor in avoidable harm; no closed-loop audit of intermittent auscultation frequency is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.2.9 (2017, amended 2026)
standard.wording: Offer women with a low risk of complications, fetal heart rate monitoring with intermittent auscultation when in established first stage of labour. Do this as follows: ... carry out intermittent auscultation immediately after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, repeated at least once every 15 minutes, and record it as a single rate.

pass: For a woman on intermittent auscultation in established first stage, the interval between two consecutive documented auscultations does not exceed 15 minutes
population: Inclusion: low-risk women having intermittent auscultation in established first stage of labour. Exclusion: women moved to continuous CTG monitoring during the period reviewed.
sample: 40 consecutive low-risk women having intermittent auscultation in established first stage over the last 4 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a 15-minute auscultation timer into the electronic partogram that flags amber when 12 minutes have elapsed since the last entry and red at 15 minutes, visible on the ward dashboard.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward audit meeting; if the timer improves compliance, make it a permanent feature of the electronic partogram build
evidence: no closed-loop audit of intermittent auscultation frequency found in the library
pitfalls: Paper partograms with gaps in recording → exclude labours with more than 20% missing entries and note the exclusion rate
Busy labour ward staffing may make 15-minute auscultation genuinely difficult → review staffing ratios alongside the audit, not instead of the process change
Definition of 'established first stage' varies between recorders → agree the definition (4 cm plus regular contractions) with the labour ward before data collection
One midwife's caseload dominating the sample → sample across shifts and midwives
Improvement fading after the audit team moves on → make the electronic timer the permanent default rather than a temporary poster
pearls: Recruit a practice development midwife to co-lead so the change is owned by the ward, not just the audit team
Pilot the electronic timer on one bay before full roll-out to iron out false alarms
Use real (anonymised) examples of delayed auscultation from incident reports to explain the 'why' at launch
Cross-reference with the labour ward's Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK action plan so this audit is not seen as a duplicate task
Feed results back to individual midwives confidentially as well as to the team, to support learning
effort: ~25 min per 10 labours from the partogram

question: Once a woman has signs of, or is in confirmed second stage of labour, what proportion of documented intermittent auscultations were performed at least once every 5 minutes?
why: Each Baby Counts identified failure to increase the frequency of intermittent auscultation in second stage as a recurring contributory factor in intrapartum harm; this specific second-stage frequency has not had a closed-loop audit in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.2.10 (2007, amended 2026)
standard.wording: Once the woman has signs of, or is in confirmed second stage of labour: perform intermittent auscultation immediately after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, repeated at least once every 5 minutes and record it as a single rate.

pass: In second stage, the interval between two consecutive documented auscultations does not exceed 5 minutes
population: Inclusion: women on intermittent auscultation who reach second stage of labour. Exclusion: women converted to continuous CTG before or during second stage.
sample: 40 consecutive women who laboured with intermittent auscultation and reached second stage over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Partogram/electronic labour record and second stage record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a distinct 'second stage' mode to the electronic partogram auscultation timer that shortens the alert interval from 15 to 5 minutes as soon as second stage is confirmed.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward audit meeting; embed the second-stage timer mode as a permanent EPR feature if compliance improves
evidence: no closed-loop audit of second-stage intermittent auscultation frequency found in the library
pitfalls: Ambiguity about the exact moment second stage starts → use the documented time of full dilatation or bearing-down urge as the trigger, agreed in advance
Very short second stages give few data points → record the number of auscultations expected as well as achieved
Staff may confuse this with the separate first-stage 15-minute standard → make the EPR mode change explicit and visible
Retrospective note review may miss verbal-only auscultations → accept only documented entries as per protocol
Losing momentum after go-live → include the second-stage timer in new starter induction
pearls: Pair this audit with the first-stage auscultation audit so both cycles share the same data collection visit
Get labour ward coordinator sign-off on the definition of second stage onset before starting
Use huddle boards to display real-time compliance during the embedding phase
Link learning to the unit's Each Baby Counts action plan
Keep sample size and season consistent at re-audit
effort: ~25 min per 10 labours from the partogram

question: In women starting induction of labour, what proportion had a Bishop score and antenatal cardiotocography documented before the first method of induction was started?
why: Assessment before induction confirms the baby is suitable for induction and that the fetal heart rate is normal; the corpus has induction of labour practice audits [general] but no closed-loop audit of pre-induction assessment completeness.

standard.source: NICE NG207 Inducing labour, rec 1.5.1 (2008, amended 2021)
standard.wording: Ensure the position of the baby and the woman's condition are suitable for induction by: abdominally assessing the level and stability of the fetal head in the lower part of the uterus at or near the pelvic brim ... assessing and recording the Bishop score, confirming a normal fetal heart rate pattern using antenatal cardiotocography interpretation, confirming the absence of significant uterine contractions (not Braxton-Hicks) using cardiotocography.

pass: A Bishop score and a CTG confirming a normal fetal heart rate pattern are both documented in the notes before the first induction method (sweep excluded) is administered
population: Inclusion: all women undergoing induction of labour on the delivery suite or induction ward. Exclusion: induction started in extremis (category 1 indication) where immediate delivery supersedes assessment.
sample: 40 consecutive women started on induction of labour over the last 6-8 weeks
data_source: Induction of labour proforma and CTG trace
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Redesign the induction of labour proforma so the Bishop score box and a mandatory pre-induction CTG result field must both be completed before the first prostaglandin, balloon or amniotomy step can be signed for.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity governance meeting; if compliant, roll the redesigned proforma out across the induction ward and delivery suite
evidence: no closed-loop audit of pre-induction Bishop score and CTG assessment found in the library
pitfalls: Bishop score sometimes recorded narratively rather than as a number → accept only a numeric or component score as compliant
CTG performed but not formally reported before induction starts → require a documented category (normal/suspicious/pathological), not just a trace reference
Staff shortages leading to skipped pre-induction CTG on busy days → escalate persistent gaps to the labour ward matron
Retrospective note-finding may undercount compliance if records are split between paper and EPR → check both systems for each case
Definition drift between cycles (e.g. accepting an antenatal CTG from earlier in the day as 'pre-induction') → fix the definition (within 4 hours of starting) before cycle 1
pearls: Involve the induction ward coordinator in designing the proforma change
Pilot the new proforma for two weeks and fix obvious problems before the full re-audit
Use real anonymised delayed-recognition cases to make the case for the change at launch
Keep the same definition of 'before induction started' across both cycles
Feed back individual near-misses privately as well as team results
effort: ~20 min per 10 inductions from the induction proforma

question: In women having active management of the third stage after a vaginal birth, what proportion received the uterotonic at the correct dose and route (10 units oxytocin IM, 5 units oxytocin IV, or 5 units oxytocin plus 500 micrograms ergometrine IM)?
why: Active management substantially reduces postpartum haemorrhage, but the correct 2023-updated dose and route of oxytocin is not yet embedded everywhere; no closed-loop audit of third-stage uterotonic dose and route accuracy is in the library (carbetocin at caesarean birth is separately audited [NNA-203]).

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, rec 1.10.11 (2023)
standard.wording: For active management after vaginal birth, administer 10 units of oxytocin (by intramuscular injection), 5 units of oxytocin (by intravenous injection, see recommendation 1.10.12) or 5 units of oxytocin plus 500 micrograms of ergometrine (by intramuscular injection) immediately after the birth of the baby and before the cord is clamped and cut.

pass: The uterotonic given for active management is one of the three NICE-specified dose/route combinations, given after the birth of the baby and before the cord is clamped and cut
population: Inclusion: women having a vaginal birth who chose active management of the third stage. Exclusion: physiological management, caesarean births.
sample: 40 consecutive vaginal births with active third-stage management over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Birth register/electronic labour record drug administration entries
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Replace the third-stage drug chart pre-print with the three NICE-approved oxytocin/ergometrine dose-route options only, removing any legacy non-standard options.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward drug safety meeting; if compliant, standardise the pre-print across all birth settings including the midwifery-led unit
evidence: no closed-loop audit of active third-stage uterotonic dose and route accuracy found in the library
pitfalls: Legacy local practice (e.g. syntometrine as default) may persist after guidance changes → communicate the 2023 update explicitly to all grades of staff
Documentation of exact time relative to cord clamping is often absent → add a simple tick box rather than relying on free text
Small numbers if the maternity unit has a low birth rate → extend the collection period
Staff may conflate this with the caesarean carbetocin standard → make clear this audit is for vaginal births only
Improvement fading if the old pre-printed chart re-enters stock → destroy old stock once the new chart is live
pearls: Involve the labour ward pharmacist in redesigning the drug chart
Brief anaesthetic and obstetric staff as well as midwives, since doctors sometimes give the third-stage drug at instrumental births
Use a short teaching huddle to explain the rationale for the 2023 change (reduced side-effect burden with single-agent oxytocin where appropriate)
Display current compliance on the labour ward safety board
Keep the same definition of 'active management' between cycles
effort: ~20 min per 10 births from the birth register

question: In women with continuing postpartum haemorrhage who required a second-line uterotonic, what proportion also received intravenous tranexamic acid 1g given over 10 minutes?
why: Tranexamic acid reduces bleeding-related death in postpartum haemorrhage, but its use alongside uterotonics is not consistently documented; no closed-loop audit of tranexamic acid use in postpartum haemorrhage is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, rec 1.10.35 (2023)
standard.wording: In addition to uterotonic drugs, give tranexamic acid (1 g by intravenous injection over 10 minutes). Repeat if necessary after at least 30 minutes for managing continuing postpartum haemorrhage.

pass: Tranexamic acid 1g IV over 10 minutes is given alongside uterotonic drugs for continuing postpartum haemorrhage, with a repeat dose after at least 30 minutes if bleeding continues
population: Inclusion: all women with a postpartum haemorrhage of 500ml or more who received a second-line uterotonic for continuing bleeding. Exclusion: haemorrhage that resolved with a single uterotonic dose alone.
sample: 30 consecutive women with continuing postpartum haemorrhage requiring a second-line uterotonic over the last 6 months
data_source: Maternity emergency drug chart, PPH proforma, incident report
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a pre-filled tranexamic acid 1g IV line to the maternity haemorrhage emergency box drug card and the PPH proforma, so it is prescribed at the same time as the second-line uterotonic.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at maternity risk management/patient safety meeting; if compliant, embed the tranexamic acid line in the PPH simulation drill checklist
evidence: no closed-loop audit of tranexamic acid use in postpartum haemorrhage found in the library
pitfalls: PPH events are relatively infrequent → extend the collection window to 6 months to reach an adequate sample
Emergency documentation is often incomplete under pressure → use a structured PPH proforma with timed boxes rather than free text
Staff may not know the correct infusion time (10 minutes, not a rapid push) → include this explicitly in PPH drills
Ambiguity about what counts as 'continuing' haemorrhage → define as bleeding continuing after the first uterotonic dose, agreed with the labour ward before cycle 1
Fading compliance once the initial drill enthusiasm passes → repeat PPH simulation drills quarterly with tranexamic acid timing as a scored item
pearls: Link this audit to the unit's regular PPH simulation training programme
Involve the obstetric anaesthetist and transfusion practitioner as co-investigators
Use the maternity haemorrhage box contents check as a natural trigger to review the drug card design
Present near-miss and good-practice cases anonymously at multidisciplinary training
Keep the same PPH volume threshold and definition of 'continuing' bleeding at re-audit
effort: ~20 min per case from the PPH proforma and drug chart

question: In births with active management of the third stage, what proportion had the exact time of cord clamping recorded, and was the cord clamped no earlier than 1 minute and before 5 minutes from birth?
why: NICE requires the timing of cord clamping to be recorded in every birth and specifies a window for active management, but this is inconsistently documented outside the preterm cord-clamping pathway already audited in the library [NNA-198]; no audit of cord-clamping timing documentation for term active-managed births exists.

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, recs 1.10.14 and 1.10.16 (2014, amended 2023)
standard.wording: After administering the uterotonic, clamp and cut the cord, but: do not clamp the cord earlier than 1 minute from the birth of the baby unless there is concern about the integrity of the cord or the baby has a heart rate below 60 beats a minute that is not getting faster; clamp the cord before 5 minutes in order to perform controlled cord traction as part of active management ... Record the timing of cord clamping in both active and physiological management.

pass: The time of cord clamping is documented, and clamping occurred at or after 1 minute and before 5 minutes from birth (unless a documented clinical reason for earlier clamping is recorded)
population: Inclusion: term births with active management of the third stage. Exclusion: preterm births below 37 weeks (covered by the existing preterm cord-clamping audit), stillbirths.
sample: 40 consecutive term vaginal births with active third-stage management over the last 4 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'time of cord clamping' field, with an automatic timer started at the recorded time of birth, to the electronic birth record for every vaginal birth.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward audit meeting; if compliant, extend the automatic timer field to caesarean birth records
evidence: [NNA-198] preterm cord clamping is separately audited in the proposed library
no audit of term cord-clamping timing documentation found in the library
pitfalls: Cord clamping time is often estimated rather than timed → provide a wall clock or timer visible to the person clamping the cord
Staff may confuse this with the preterm cord-clamping standard → make clear in training that this audit covers term active-managed births
Retrospective note review may find blank fields rather than wrong values → record 'not documented' as a distinct category, not a fail by default, to identify where the gap is
Genuine clinical reasons for early clamping (cord integrity concern, poor condition at birth) must not be miscounted as non-compliance → capture the documented reason
Fading compliance after go-live → include the field in the maternity dashboard so gaps are visible weekly
pearls: Use a simple wall-mounted timer or the delivery room clock as a low-cost prompt
Recruit maternity support workers to help time and record cord clamping during the collection period
Link this audit with training on delayed cord clamping benefits for haemoglobin and iron stores
Present compliance trends, not just a single snapshot, to the labour ward forum
Keep the same window definition (1-5 minutes) and exclusions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 births from the birth register

question: What proportion of babies had uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact with their mother (or birth companion if the mother was unable) started within 5 minutes of birth and continued for at least the first hour, with no separation for routine procedures during that time?
why: Early, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact supports thermoregulation, breastfeeding initiation and bonding, but routine weighing and measuring often interrupt it; no closed-loop audit of skin-to-skin contact timing and duration is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, recs 1.11.7 and 1.11.10 (2007, amended 2023)
standard.wording: Encourage women to have skin-to-skin contact with their babies as soon as possible after the birth. If the woman is not well enough, encourage her birth companion to have skin-to-skin contact instead. ... Avoid separating the woman and her baby within the first hour of the birth for routine postnatal procedures, for example, weighing, measuring and bathing, unless these measures are requested by the woman or are necessary for the immediate care of the baby.

pass: Skin-to-skin contact is documented as starting within 5 minutes of birth and continuing uninterrupted for at least 1 hour, with no routine procedure documented as the reason for any earlier separation
population: Inclusion: all live births on the labour ward and midwifery-led unit where the baby did not need resuscitation. Exclusion: babies needing resuscitation or immediate neonatal unit admission.
sample: 40 consecutive births not requiring neonatal resuscitation over the last 4 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'skin-to-skin start and end time' box to the birth record and move routine weighing/measuring to after the first postnatal hour in the ward's standard birth checklist.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the infant feeding and maternity governance meetings; if compliant, embed the revised checklist order across all birth settings
evidence: no closed-loop audit of skin-to-skin contact timing and interruption found in the library
pitfalls: Skin-to-skin start/stop times are rarely documented precisely → accept nearest 5-minute estimates and note this limitation
Genuine clinical reasons for interruption (maternal instability, baby needing review) must not be counted as non-compliance → capture the documented reason
Staff habit of weighing the baby immediately is hard to change → involve maternity support workers, who usually do the weighing, in redesigning the checklist
Caesarean births may need a separate pathway (theatre staffing, recovery) → consider auditing vaginal and caesarean births separately
Improvement fading if the checklist reverts to the old order → update the printed and electronic checklist together
pearls: Involve an infant feeding lead/lactation consultant as co-investigator
Use UNICEF Baby Friendly Initiative standards as a familiar framework for staff
Display compliance alongside breastfeeding initiation rates, since the two are linked
Consider a champion on each shift to model early, uninterrupted skin-to-skin
Keep exclusions (resuscitation, neonatal unit admission) identical at re-audit
effort: ~20 min per 10 births from the birth register

question: What proportion of babies had a parental decision about vitamin K prophylaxis (accepted by injection, accepted orally, or declined) recorded before transfer from the birth setting?
why: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding is rare but preventable, and NICE 2026 guidance reintroduced explicit reference to vitamin K prophylaxis; no closed-loop audit of vitamin K decision documentation is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, rec 1.11.12 (2006, amended 2026)
standard.wording: Offer parents vitamin K prophylaxis for their babies. Explain this is to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which is a rare but serious and sometimes fatal disorder.

pass: A vitamin K decision (accepted by injection, accepted orally with a documented follow-up plan, or declined) is recorded in the baby's notes before transfer from the birth setting
population: Inclusion: all live births. Exclusion: babies transferred directly to the neonatal unit before the discussion could take place.
sample: 40 consecutive live births over the last 4 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'vitamin K discussed and decision recorded' field to the electronic newborn discharge checklist that must be completed before the birth episode can be closed.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity governance meeting; if compliant, make the field a hard stop in the EPR discharge workflow
evidence: no closed-loop audit of vitamin K decision documentation found in the library
pitfalls: Vitamin K given but not documented, understating true practice → cross-check the drug administration record as well as the discharge checklist
Oral vitamin K needs multiple doses and a follow-up plan, which is often the part left undocumented → make follow-up plan a required sub-field, not just 'oral given'
Parents declining vitamin K may not have this decision recorded, only omission → make 'declined' an explicit selectable option, not a blank
Home births and midwifery-led unit births may use different documentation → include both settings in the sample
Improvement fading without a hard stop → build the field into the EPR rather than a paper checklist alone
pearls: Agree the exact wording of the three decision options with the neonatal team before cycle 1
Use a short scripted explanation for staff to give consistent information to parents
Cross-check a sample against the drug administration record to validate documentation accuracy
Involve postnatal ward staff, since some decisions are made after transfer from the birth room
Keep the same three decision categories at re-audit for comparability
effort: ~15 min per 10 births from the newborn record

question: What proportion of women who had an instrumental vaginal birth (forceps or ventouse) received a single dose of intravenous co-amoxiclav (or a locally agreed alternative) within 6 hours after cord clamping?
why: A single prophylactic antibiotic dose after instrumental birth reduces maternal infection, but timing and completion are not routinely checked; no closed-loop audit of post-instrumental-birth antibiotic prophylaxis is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, rec 1.9.43 (2023)
standard.wording: Offer women who have had a birth with forceps or ventouse a single dose of intravenous co-amoxiclav (or a locally agreed alternative for women who are allergic to penicillin) within 6 hours after cord clamping.

pass: A single dose of IV co-amoxiclav (or the locally agreed penicillin-allergy alternative) is prescribed and administered within 6 hours of cord clamping
population: Inclusion: all women having a forceps or ventouse birth. Exclusion: women already on therapeutic antibiotics for another indication.
sample: 40 consecutive instrumental vaginal births over the last 6-8 weeks
data_source: Electronic drug chart and birth record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a pre-filled 'co-amoxiclav 1.2g IV, single dose, within 6 hours of instrumental birth' order set to the electronic prescribing system, triggered when the birth mode is coded as forceps or ventouse.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at maternity medicines safety meeting; if compliant, review at 6 months for sustained compliance
evidence: no closed-loop audit of post-instrumental-birth antibiotic prophylaxis timing found in the library
pitfalls: Instrumental births at night or in an emergency may have prophylaxis forgotten → include an automatic EPR prompt rather than relying on memory
Penicillin allergy alternatives vary between trusts → confirm the local alternative with pharmacy before starting
Time from cord clamping (not from birth of baby) may be poorly documented → accept birth time as a proxy where clamping time is missing and note the limitation
Antibiotic prescribed but not actually administered within the window → check both prescribing and administration records
Fading compliance once the initial launch attention passes → include compliance in the routine maternity medicines dashboard
pearls: Involve the labour ward pharmacist in building the order set
Brief the on-call obstetric team as well as midwives, since doctors usually perform instrumental births
Use theatre/instrumental birth trolleys to physically prompt the antibiotic dose
Track reasons for non-administration (e.g. declined, allergy uncertainty) to target further work
Keep the same 6-hour window and instrument definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 births from the drug chart

question: What proportion of babies had a complete newborn and infant physical examination (NIPE) documented within 72 hours of birth?
why: The 72-hour newborn examination detects major abnormalities early, but completion within the national timeframe is not routinely audited outside the specific hip-screening pathway already in the library [ONA-060, ONA-061]; no audit of overall 72-hour NIPE completion exists.

standard.source: NICE NG194 Postnatal care, rec 1.3.3 (2021)
standard.wording: Carry out a complete examination of the baby within 72 hours of the birth and at 6 to 8 weeks after the birth (see the NHS newborn and infant physical examination [NIPE] screening programme).

pass: The full NIPE examination (all systems listed in NG194 1.3.3) is documented as completed within 72 hours of birth
population: Inclusion: all babies born in the unit or transferred home within the maternity service's care. Exclusion: babies who died before 72 hours, babies transferred to another provider before examination.
sample: 40 consecutive babies born over the last 4 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'NIPE due by' countdown (birth time plus 72 hours) to the postnatal ward whiteboard/EPR task list, visible to the team booking discharges.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the neonatal/maternity governance meeting; if compliant, extend the countdown prompt to home births and early transfers
evidence: [ONA-060] and [ONA-061] audit the downstream hip-screening pathway; no audit of overall 72-hour NIPE completion found in the library
pitfalls: Early transfer home or short postnatal stay can make the 72-hour window difficult → flag these babies for a home or GP-arranged NIPE and track separately
NIPE performed but recorded on paper not in the electronic system → check both records before counting as not done
Staffing gaps (no NIPE-trained practitioner on a shift) causing delay → escalate rota gaps to the neonatal/paediatric lead
Partial examinations (e.g. hips only) may be miscounted as complete → require all listed systems to be documented
Improvement fading after go-live → include NIPE completion in the daily safety huddle metrics
pearls: Recruit the NIPE lead practitioner as co-investigator
Use the existing electronic NIPE screening record as the primary data source to minimise extra work
Cross-check timing against discharge time to identify babies discharged before examination
Share compliance weekly with the postnatal ward as a visible metric
Keep the 72-hour definition and exclusions identical at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 babies from the NIPE screening record

question: At each postnatal contact in the first 6-8 weeks, what proportion of women had their psychological and emotional wellbeing formally assessed and documented?
why: Routine assessment of mood at every postnatal contact is a distinct NICE requirement from the written perinatal care plan for women with severe mental illness already audited in the library [NNA-163]; no audit of routine mood assessment at every postnatal contact exists.

standard.source: NICE NG194 Postnatal care, rec 1.2.x 'Recognising mental health problems' section (2021)
standard.wording: At each postnatal contact, assess the woman's psychological and emotional wellbeing. Follow the recommendations on recognising mental health problems in pregnancy and the postnatal period and referral in the NICE guideline on antenatal and postnatal mental health. If there are concerns, arrange for further assessment and follow up.

pass: Each documented postnatal contact includes a recorded psychological/emotional wellbeing assessment, with a follow-up plan recorded whenever concerns are noted
population: Inclusion: all women having community postnatal contacts in the first 6-8 weeks. Exclusion: women who declined a postnatal contact.
sample: 40 consecutive women, reviewing all postnatal contacts up to the 6-8 week check, over the last 6 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory mood/emotional wellbeing assessment field to every postnatal contact template in the community electronic record, which must be completed before the contact can be closed.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the community midwifery and perinatal mental health governance meeting; if compliant, extend the mandatory field to health visitor contact templates
evidence: [NNA-163] audits the written care plan for severe mental illness; no audit of routine mood assessment at every postnatal contact found in the library
pitfalls: Mood assessment sometimes recorded narratively without a clear structure → agree a minimum structured question set (for example, the two Whooley questions) before cycle 1
Contacts done by phone may be less thoroughly documented than face-to-face → record contact type and compare compliance by type
Women lost to follow-up (moved, discharged early) reduce the denominator → record and report separately, not as non-compliance
Staff may feel this duplicates the perinatal mental health screening already done antenatally → explain this is about ongoing postnatal review, not booking screening
Improvement fading without a mandatory field → make the field compulsory in the EPR rather than an optional free-text box
pearls: Involve the perinatal mental health midwife lead as co-investigator
Use a validated brief tool (Whooley questions or Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) consistently across the team
Feed back individual practitioner compliance sensitively alongside team-level results
Link this audit to the trust's perinatal mental health strategy and MBRRACE-UK maternal death recommendations
Keep the same assessment tool and contact definitions at re-audit
effort: ~20 min per 10 women from the community postnatal record

question: What proportion of postnatal discharge records document that the baby had passed meconium within 24 hours of birth, or that a medical review was arranged if not?
why: Failure to pass meconium within 24 hours can indicate a serious underlying disorder such as Hirschsprung's disease or anorectal malformation; there is no closed-loop audit in the library of this specific safety-netting check before discharge.

standard.source: NICE NG194 Postnatal care, rec 1.3.2 (2021)
standard.wording: Be aware that if the baby has not passed meconium within 24 hours of birth, this may indicate a serious disorder and requires medical advice.

pass: The discharge or 24-hour check record documents either that meconium has passed, or, if not, that medical advice/review was sought before discharge
population: Inclusion: all babies discharged from the birth setting within 48 hours. Exclusion: babies remaining as neonatal unit inpatients beyond 24 hours for an unrelated reason.
sample: 40 consecutive babies discharged within 48 hours of birth over the last 4 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'meconium passed by 24 hours: yes/no/pending review' field to the electronic discharge checklist that must be completed before discharge is signed off.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the postnatal ward safety huddle; if compliant, extend the field to the home birth discharge checklist
evidence: no closed-loop audit of meconium passage safety-netting before discharge found in the library
pitfalls: Meconium passage is often not asked about directly, only inferred from nappy charts → make it an explicit yes/no question at discharge
Early discharge before 24 hours makes assessment impossible at the point of discharge → record a safety-netting plan (what to look for, who to contact) for these babies instead
Staff may assume a normal-looking baby has passed meconium without checking → require a positive confirmation, not an assumption
Retrospective note review may miss verbal advice given without documentation → count only documented safety-netting as compliant
Improvement fading without a mandatory field → build it into the EPR discharge workflow
pearls: Combine this check with the existing discharge checklist review to avoid extra staff workload
Train maternity support workers, who often complete nappy/feeding charts, to flag meconium status
Use a simple laminated prompt card on the postnatal ward during the embedding phase
Share any missed or delayed diagnoses (anonymised) at induction/mandatory training to reinforce the rationale
Keep the same 24-hour definition and discharge timing categories at re-audit
effort: ~10 min per 10 babies from the discharge checklist

question: What proportion of women had a documented venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk assessment at their antenatal booking appointment?
why: VTE remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in the UK, and a documented early risk assessment is the foundation of thromboprophylaxis decisions; no closed-loop audit of booking VTE risk assessment completion is in the library.

standard.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37a, Reducing the Risk of Venous Thromboembolism during Pregnancy and the Puerperium (April 2015, amended 2023), Executive summary of recommendations
standard.wording: All women should undergo a documented assessment of risk factors for VTE in early pregnancy or prepregnancy.

pass: A structured VTE risk assessment (using the local or national scoring tool) is completed and documented in the notes at the booking appointment
population: Inclusion: all women booking for antenatal care. Exclusion: women booking after 20 weeks whose first contact was an emergency admission.
sample: 40 consecutive women at their booking appointment over the last 4 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make the structured VTE risk assessment tool a mandatory, non-skippable section of the electronic booking proforma.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity governance and thrombosis committee meeting; if compliant, extend mandatory reassessment fields to hospital admission during pregnancy
evidence: no closed-loop audit of booking VTE risk assessment completion found in the library
pitfalls: Booking appointments are sometimes done by different staff groups (GP, community midwife) with different systems → confirm which system captures the assessment before cycle 1
Risk assessment done verbally but not documented → count only documented assessments as compliant
Missing risk factors (e.g. undocumented BMI or family history) can make the assessment incomplete even if a form was started → check completeness, not just presence of a form
Women booking late or via unbooked emergency attendance are hard to capture → report this group separately
Improvement fading if the mandatory field can be bypassed → confirm the EPR build genuinely blocks completion of booking without it
pearls: Involve the maternity thrombosis lead midwife/obstetrician as co-investigator
Use the RCOG/local VTE risk assessment tool your unit has already adopted, for consistency
Cross-check a sample of high-risk women to confirm the resulting thromboprophylaxis plan was actually carried out
Present findings alongside MBRRACE-UK data on VTE as a leading cause of direct maternal death, to support engagement
Keep the same risk assessment tool and definition of 'booking' at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the booking record

question: What proportion of women having a vaginal birth had a systematic perineal examination, including a digital rectal examination, documented before perineal suturing?
why: Undiagnosed obstetric anal sphincter injury causes long-term incontinence; systematic examination including a rectal examination is a core element of the national OASI care bundle, but is not consistently documented; no closed-loop audit of this specific step is in the library (perineal repair pain relief is separately audited [NNA-205, NNA-206]).

standard.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 29, The Management of Third- and Fourth-Degree Perineal Tears (2015)
standard.wording: All women having a vaginal delivery are at risk of sustaining OASIS or isolated rectal buttonhole tears. They should therefore be examined systematically, including a digital rectal examination, to assess the severity of damage, particularly prior to suturing.

pass: The perineal examination record documents a systematic assessment including a digital rectal examination, completed before suturing began
population: Inclusion: all women having a vaginal birth with any degree of perineal trauma. Exclusion: women with an intact perineum and no trauma.
sample: 40 consecutive vaginal births with perineal trauma over the last 4-6 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Redesign the perineal repair record as a structured proforma with a mandatory digital rectal examination tick box that must be completed before the suturing section can be signed.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the OASI care bundle/maternity governance meeting; if compliant, roll the proforma out to the midwifery-led unit
evidence: no closed-loop audit of systematic perineal/rectal examination documentation found in the library
pitfalls: Rectal examination may be performed but not documented → accept only documented examination as compliant; consider a spot-check with the woman's consent if under-recording is suspected
Junior staff may be uncomfortable performing or documenting a rectal examination → provide OASI care bundle training and supervision
Free-text notes may describe the tear without confirming a rectal examination was done → use a structured tick-box proforma rather than free text
Under-recognition of OASI, not just under-documentation, is the real risk → track third/fourth-degree tear detection rates alongside documentation compliance
Improvement fading without embedding in training → include the proforma in annual perineal repair skills updates
pearls: Base the audit on the national OASI care bundle project methodology so results are comparable with other units
Involve the OASI care bundle champion or perineal trauma lead as co-investigator
Use simulation training (perineal repair mannequins) to reinforce the systematic examination technique
Track OASI detection rate as a linked outcome measure alongside documentation compliance
Keep the same tear degree categories and examiner grade field at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 births from the perineal repair record

question: Of instrumental vaginal births with a mediolateral episiotomy, what proportion had the episiotomy angle documented as approximately 60 degrees from the midline at the time of distension?
why: An episiotomy cut too close to the midline increases the risk of extension into the anal sphincter; angle documentation is a core OASI care bundle element but is inconsistently recorded; no closed-loop audit of episiotomy angle documentation is in the library.

standard.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 29, The Management of Third- and Fourth-Degree Perineal Tears (2015)
standard.wording: Where episiotomy is indicated, the mediolateral technique is recommended, with careful attention to ensure that the angle is 60 degrees away from the midline when the perineum is distended.

pass: The birth record documents that a mediolateral episiotomy was performed and states the angle achieved (or confirms the 60-degree technique was used) at the time of distension
population: Inclusion: all instrumental vaginal births (forceps or ventouse) with an episiotomy. Exclusion: spontaneous vaginal births without instrumental delivery.
sample: 40 consecutive instrumental births with episiotomy over the last 6-8 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce an episiotomy angle guide (a single-use disposable protractor/angle indicator) at every instrumental birth, with a mandatory 'angle achieved' field on the instrumental birth proforma.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the OASI care bundle meeting; if compliant, extend the angle guide to spontaneous births requiring episiotomy
evidence: no closed-loop audit of mediolateral episiotomy angle documentation found in the library
pitfalls: Angle is difficult to measure precisely in a fast-moving birth → accept a disposable angle-guide indicator mark as a reasonable proxy for documentation
Only the mediolateral technique should be counted; midline episiotomy carries a higher OASI risk and should be flagged separately → record technique type explicitly
Junior obstetric and midwifery staff performing episiotomies may lack confidence with angle guides → provide simulation training before roll-out
Retrospective note review may only capture 'episiotomy performed' without angle detail → introduce the field prospectively for cycle 2
Improvement fading if angle guides run out of stock → confirm reliable procurement before wider roll-out
pearls: Use the same OASI care bundle framework and champion as the rectal-examination audit above, since they share a data collection visit
Pilot the angle guide with a small group of obstetricians and senior midwives first
Track OASI rate alongside angle-guide use as the outcome measure
Share results with the local perineal trauma multidisciplinary meeting
Keep the same technique and angle definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 births from the instrumental delivery proforma

question: What proportion of women presenting with reduced fetal movements after 26 weeks had fetal heart rate auscultation, symphysis-fundal height/growth review and a fetal heart rate assessment (CTG) all completed and documented at that presentation, in line with the national RFM checklist?
why: Unrecognised or poorly managed reduced fetal movements (RFM) is a recurring contributory factor in avoidable stillbirth identified by MBRRACE-UK; no closed-loop audit of full RFM checklist completion is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 3, 'Suggested checklist for the management of reduced fetal movements (RFM)' (2023)
standard.wording: 2. Act: Auscultate fetal heart (hand-held Doppler/Pinnard) to confirm fetal viability. Assess fetal growth by reviewing growth chart, perform SFH if not performed within last 2 weeks (if not on an ultrasound surveillance pathway already). Perform CTG to assess fetal heart rate in accordance with national guidelines (ideally computerised CTG should be used).

pass: At the RFM presentation, fetal heart rate auscultation, a fundal height/growth review (or confirmation of an existing surveillance scan within 2 weeks) and a CTG are all documented as completed
population: Inclusion: all women presenting to triage or the day assessment unit with reduced fetal movements after 26 weeks. Exclusion: women presenting in established labour.
sample: 40 consecutive women presenting with reduced fetal movements over the last 4-6 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a structured RFM triage proforma based on the national Ask-Act-Advise checklist, with all three Act steps as mandatory fields before the assessment can be closed.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity safety champions meeting; if compliant, embed the proforma as the standard triage RFM pathway
evidence: no closed-loop audit of full reduced fetal movements checklist completion found in the library
pitfalls: RFM presentations are often managed hastily on a busy triage shift → make the proforma the fastest route, not an extra step, by pre-populating fields from the booking record
Recurrent RFM (which carries higher risk) may not be flagged if previous episodes are not cross-referenced → build a search of previous RFM presentations into the proforma
Growth chart review is sometimes skipped if a scan was 'recent' without checking the exact date → require the date of the last scan to be entered
Staff unfamiliar with the national checklist → provide short RFM update training before cycle 1
Improvement fading without an EPR-embedded proforma → build the checklist into the triage EPR template, not a paper insert
pearls: Base the audit directly on the NHS England SBLCB v3 checklist so it aligns with national reporting
Involve the maternity safety champion and RFM/stillbirth prevention lead as co-investigators
Track induction of labour and caesarean birth rates alongside compliance to watch for unintended over-intervention
Use anonymised MBRRACE-UK case summaries in training to explain the rationale
Keep the same first/recurrent RFM definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 presentations from the triage record

question: Of pregnant women identified as smokers and referred for tobacco dependence treatment, what proportion were contacted within 1 working day and seen face-to-face by a tobacco dependence adviser within 5 working days of referral?
why: Rapid opt-out referral to tobacco dependence treatment is central to reducing smoking in pregnancy, but referral-to-contact timeliness is not routinely tracked; no closed-loop audit of this specific timeliness standard is in the library (CO testing itself is already audited [NNA-195]).

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 1 implementation guidance, 'Opt-out referral pathways' (2023)
standard.wording: Immediate referral and consultation with the tobacco dependence adviser is the ideal, but as a minimum the woman should be contacted within 1 working day and seen (ideally face-to-face) by a TDA within 5 working days.

pass: The woman is contacted by the tobacco dependence service within 1 working day of referral and seen face-to-face within 5 working days
population: Inclusion: all pregnant women with an opt-out referral to the in-house tobacco dependence treatment service. Exclusion: women who self-refer outside the opt-out pathway.
sample: 40 consecutive opt-out tobacco dependence referrals over the last 8-12 weeks
data_source: Tobacco dependence service referral and contact log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set up an automatic same-day electronic referral from the maternity CO-testing record straight into the tobacco dependence adviser's worklist, replacing any manual fax or paper referral step.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity smoking in pregnancy steering group; if compliant, use the electronic referral pathway as the trust standard
evidence: [NNA-195] audits CO/smoking status recording; no audit of referral-to-contact timeliness for the tobacco dependence service found in the library
pitfalls: Referral date and contact date are sometimes recorded in different systems → agree a single source of truth (the tobacco dependence service log) before cycle 1
Working days versus calendar days can be miscounted around weekends and bank holidays → define clearly and apply consistently
Women who decline contact should not be miscounted as a service delay → record 'declined contact' as a distinct outcome
Small tobacco dependence adviser team capacity may be the real bottleneck → report capacity alongside timeliness data to inform service planning
Improvement fading if referrals revert to a manual process → confirm the electronic referral route is the permanent default
pearls: Involve the tobacco dependence adviser team directly, since they hold the contact log
Benchmark local performance against the Maternity Services Dashboard smoking metrics
Track quit-date setting and 4-week quit rates alongside timeliness as a linked outcome
Present results at the local Smoking in Pregnancy Challenge Group network meeting for benchmarking
Keep the same working-day definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 referrals from the tobacco dependence service log

question: What proportion of women had a fetal growth restriction (FGR) risk assessment completed by 14 weeks' gestation, using a validated digital blood pressure monitor for the blood pressure component?
why: Early, structured FGR risk assessment determines the surveillance pathway a woman is offered; digital blood pressure measurement was newly mandated in the 2023 care bundle update, and no closed-loop audit of this combined standard is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 2, interventions 2.4 and 2.6 (2023)
standard.wording: 2.4 Perform a risk assessment for FGR by 14 weeks gestation using an agreed pathway (for example, Appendix D). ... 2.6 As part of the risk assessment for FGR, blood pressure should be recorded using a digital monitor that has been [validated for use in pregnancy].

pass: The FGR risk assessment is documented as completed by 14+0 weeks' gestation, and the blood pressure recorded as part of it was measured on a validated digital monitor
population: Inclusion: all women booked for antenatal care who reach 14 weeks under the unit's care. Exclusion: women booking after 14 weeks.
sample: 40 consecutive women who reached 14 weeks' gestation over the last 6-8 weeks
data_source: Antenatal booking and risk assessment record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make the FGR risk assessment pathway a mandatory field in the electronic booking record with a due-date prompt at 14 weeks, and replace remaining manual sphygmomanometers in booking clinics with validated digital monitors.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity safety champions meeting; if compliant, report ongoing compliance through the Maternity Services Dashboard
evidence: no closed-loop audit of combined 14-week FGR risk assessment and validated digital blood pressure recording found in the library
pitfalls: Booking sometimes happens after 14 weeks, making the deadline unachievable for some women → report late bookers separately, not as non-compliance
Non-validated manual sphygmomanometers may still be in use in some clinic rooms → audit equipment as well as documentation
Risk assessment pathway/tool varies locally → confirm which tool (for example, a locally agreed algorithm per Appendix D of the care bundle) is in use before cycle 1
Community midwives booking women may use a different system from the hospital → include both settings in the sample
Improvement fading if old equipment is not fully withdrawn → remove non-validated monitors from clinical areas, not just add new ones
pearls: Involve the fetal growth surveillance/screening lead midwife as co-investigator
Audit equipment (monitor validation status) at the same time as the notes review
Use the care bundle's own process indicators for benchmarking against national data
Link with community midwifery teams early since much of this assessment happens outside hospital
Keep the same risk assessment pathway and 14-week deadline definition at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the booking record

question: What proportion of midwives and obstetricians providing intrapartum care had up-to-date annual training and competency assessment in intermittent auscultation and electronic fetal monitoring?
why: Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK repeatedly cite gaps in fetal monitoring training as a contributory factor in avoidable harm; no closed-loop audit of annual fetal monitoring training completion is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 4, intervention 4.1 (2023)
standard.wording: All staff who care for women in labour are required to undertake annual training and competency assessment on knowledge and skills required for effective fetal monitoring via Intermittent auscultation (IA) [Midwives] and electronic fetal monitoring [Midwives and Obstetricians].

pass: The staff member has a documented, in-date (within the last 12 months) fetal monitoring training and competency assessment record
population: Inclusion: all midwives and obstetricians who provide intrapartum care, including bank/agency and locum staff. Exclusion: staff on long-term leave for the full audit period.
sample: All midwives and obstetricians providing intrapartum care on the unit at the time of the audit (or 40 consecutive staff records if the unit is very large)
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set up an automatic training system alert to staff and their line manager 6 weeks before their fetal monitoring training expires, and block rostering onto the labour ward for staff more than 4 weeks overdue.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity education and governance meeting; if compliant, use the alert system as the trust-wide model for other mandatory training
evidence: no closed-loop audit of annual fetal monitoring training and competency assessment completion found in the library
pitfalls: Bank, agency and locum staff are hardest to track and often missed by the trust's own training system → include a specific check for these staff groups at ward entry
Training completion recorded but competency assessment (a separate step) not done → audit both fields, not just attendance
Staff on leave (maternity, sickness) may appear overdue through no fault of their own → exclude or flag separately
Different training records systems for medical and midwifery staff can under- or double-count → reconcile both systems before reporting
Improvement fading without automatic alerts → confirm the alert system, not just a spreadsheet, is doing the tracking
pearls: Involve the practice development midwife/fetal monitoring lead and medical education lead as co-investigators
Use existing trust training system reports as the primary data source to avoid duplicate data entry
Report compliance by staff group so gaps (for example, obstetric trainees rotating in) are visible
Link training compliance data to the unit's Each Baby Counts and SBLCB v3 annual submission
Keep the same 12-month in-date definition at re-audit
effort: ~10 min per 10 staff records from the training system

question: What proportion of women with pre-existing diabetes had an HbA1c measured at the start of the third trimester, with a documented increased-surveillance plan if the result was above 48 mmol/mol?
why: Women with type 1 and type 2 diabetes continue to have persistently high perinatal mortality; third-trimester HbA1c monitoring with escalation is a new 2023 care bundle standard with no closed-loop audit yet in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 6, intervention 6.4 (2023)
standard.wording: Women with diabetes should have an HbA1c measured at the start of the third trimester and those with an HbA1c above 48mmol/mmol should be offered increased surveillance including additional diabetes nurse/dietetic support, more frequent face to face review and input from their named, specialist Consultant to plan ongoing care and timing of birth decisions.

pass: An HbA1c is recorded at 28+0 to 28+6 weeks (start of third trimester), and if above 48 mmol/mol, an increased-surveillance plan is documented
population: Inclusion: all women with pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes under joint diabetes-obstetric care. Exclusion: women diagnosed with gestational diabetes only.
sample: 30 consecutive women with pre-existing diabetes reaching the third trimester over the last 3-6 months
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic HbA1c order and a due-date prompt at 28 weeks to the joint diabetes antenatal clinic pathway, with a mandatory 'surveillance plan' field triggered when the result exceeds 48 mmol/mol.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint diabetes-obstetric MDT and the National Pregnancy in Diabetes (NPID) audit review meeting; if compliant, submit the improved pathway as evidence to the NPID audit
evidence: no closed-loop audit of third-trimester HbA1c monitoring and escalation for pre-existing diabetes in pregnancy found in the library
pitfalls: Women with diabetes are a relatively small cohort per unit → extend the collection period to 3-6 months to reach an adequate sample
HbA1c may be requested but the result not reviewed or acted on → audit the surveillance plan, not just the blood test being done
Joint clinic records may be split between diabetes and obstetric systems → check both before concluding non-compliance
Definition of 'increased surveillance' varies between clinicians → agree a minimum data set (extra visit booked, dietitian/diabetes nurse referral, named consultant documented) before cycle 1
Improvement fading without an automatic order → build the 28-week HbA1c into the standard order set, not a manual reminder
pearls: Involve the joint diabetes antenatal clinic team (diabetes consultant, specialist nurse, dietitian) as co-investigators
Submit results to the National Pregnancy in Diabetes (NPID) audit for external benchmarking
Use the multidisciplinary joint clinic list as the sampling frame to minimise missed cases
Present findings against the unit's overall SBLCB v3 element 6 compliance
Keep the same 48 mmol/mol threshold and 28-week timing at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the joint diabetes clinic record

question: What proportion of babies born before 34 weeks' gestation had their first temperature recorded between 36.5 and 37.5 degrees Celsius, measured within one hour of birth?
why: Neonatal hypothermia after preterm birth increases the risk of death and morbidity; normothermia is a scored element of the national perinatal optimisation pathway but is not yet separately audited in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 5, Normothermia (2023)
standard.wording: Babies born at less than 37 weeks gestational age should have a first temperature which is both between 36.5–37.5°C and measured within one hour of birth. Neonatal normothermia can have benefits for all babies.

pass: The baby's first recorded temperature is between 36.5 and 37.5 degrees Celsius and was measured within 1 hour of birth
population: Inclusion: all babies born before 34 weeks' gestation. Exclusion: stillbirths, babies who died before a temperature could be recorded.
sample: 30 consecutive babies born before 34 weeks over the last 6 months
data_source: Neonatal admission record/delivery room resuscitation record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a preterm delivery normothermia bundle (pre-warmed delivery room, polythene wrap/hat, transwarmer mattress) as a standard checklist item for every birth under 34 weeks, based on the BAPM normothermia toolkit.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the neonatal/perinatal optimisation pathway meeting; if compliant, report through the National Neonatal Audit Programme (NNAP) normothermia measure
evidence: no closed-loop audit of preterm normothermia (temperature target and timing) found in the library
pitfalls: Very preterm births are relatively infrequent → extend the collection period to 6 months and use network-level data if the unit's numbers are too small
Temperature taken later than 1 hour may be recorded without the delay being obvious → record both the time and the value
Emergency preterm births may not allow time for the full normothermia bundle to be prepared → record whether the birth was planned or emergency and compare
Different thermometers/sites (axillary vs other) can give inconsistent readings → standardise the measurement method across the unit
Improvement fading without embedding → make the normothermia bundle a standing item on the preterm birth checklist, not a one-off initiative
pearls: Base the change directly on the BAPM normothermia toolkit for a ready-made implementation package
Involve neonatal nursing staff and the labour ward as joint owners, since both are responsible for temperature control
Benchmark against National Neonatal Audit Programme (NNAP) data
Link this audit to the wider perinatal optimisation pathway compliance metric in the care bundle
Keep the same gestation cut-off and timing definition at re-audit
effort: ~10 min per 10 babies from the neonatal admission record

question: What proportion of babies born before 34 weeks' gestation received their own mother's milk within 24 hours of birth?
why: Early maternal breast milk reduces necrotising enterocolitis and late-onset sepsis in preterm babies; this is a scored perinatal optimisation pathway element with no closed-loop audit yet in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 5, Early maternal breast milk (2023)
standard.wording: Babies born below 37 weeks gestational age should receive their own mother's milk, ideally within 6 hours, but aiming always within 24 hours of birth (except in rare situations where there are contraindications to MBM). Perinatal teams should work together to ensure consistent delivery of antenatal advice about MBM, with support (equipment, education, help) for mothers to express within two hours of birth.

pass: The baby receives their own mother's milk within 24 hours of birth, and the mother was supported to start expressing within 2 hours of birth, unless a documented contraindication exists
population: Inclusion: all babies born before 34 weeks' gestation. Exclusion: babies with a documented contraindication to maternal breast milk, stillbirths.
sample: 30 consecutive babies born before 34 weeks over the last 6 months
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Ensure a breast pump, expressing consumables and written/verbal expressing support are available at the mother's bedside within 2 hours of a preterm birth, prompted by a checklist item on the neonatal admission pathway.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the neonatal/infant feeding governance meeting; if compliant, report through the perinatal optimisation pathway compliance metric
evidence: no closed-loop audit of early maternal breast milk provision for preterm babies found in the library
pitfalls: Mothers recovering from caesarean birth or illness may be physically unable to express within 2 hours → record and report this separately from equipment or support failures
Milk expressed but not given to the baby promptly (e.g. delayed transport to neonatal unit) → capture both expressing time and administration time
Equipment availability (pumps, kits) at night or on a busy unit can be a genuine bottleneck → audit equipment availability alongside documentation
Small numbers of very preterm births → extend the collection period to 6 months
Improvement fading without embedding → make expressing support a standing item on the preterm admission checklist
pearls: Involve the infant feeding lead and neonatal nursing team as co-investigators
Use the BAPM maternal breast milk toolkit for a ready-made implementation package
Track necrotising enterocolitis and late-onset sepsis rates as linked longer-term outcome measures
Ensure postnatal ward and neonatal unit protocols are aligned so support does not stop at transfer

question: In babies with an acute fetal bradycardia (or a single prolonged deceleration of 3 minutes or more) that did not recover, what proportion were born within 9 minutes of the bradycardia being recognised, or had a documented reason for a longer interval?
