change: Build a structured ectopic pregnancy management decision proforma into the early pregnancy unit record with the hCG threshold and follow-up criteria as mandatory fields before expectant management can be selected.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the early pregnancy unit/gynaecology governance meeting; if compliant, review any rupture or emergency admission cases at the departmental morbidity meeting
evidence: no closed-loop audit of expectant management eligibility documentation for ectopic pregnancy found in the library
pitfalls: Ectopic pregnancy volumes are relatively low per unit → extend the collection period to 12 months
hCG result timing relative to the decision may be unclear in retrospective notes → record the hCG date and value explicitly
Women may be judged clinically stable without this being explicitly documented → require an explicit statement, not an assumption
Follow-up non-attendance is itself a safety risk requiring an escalation plan → record any non-attendance and the service's response
Fading compliance without a structured proforma → embed the eligibility fields into the decision record, not a separate audit form
pearls: Involve the early pregnancy unit lead as co-investigator
Use a dedicated ectopic pregnancy tracking log to actively follow up all expectantly managed women
Review any case of rupture or emergency surgery after expectant management at the morbidity meeting to close the loop
Give women a clear written safety-netting leaflet on symptoms of rupture
Keep the same hCG thresholds at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per case from the early pregnancy unit record

question: In women with a retained placenta, what proportion had intravenous access secured, with the reason explained to the woman, documented at the time retention was diagnosed?
why: Retained placenta carries a risk of sudden major haemorrhage; securing IV access early is a basic safety step that is not routinely checked; no closed-loop audit of this step is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, rec 1.10.21 (2014)
standard.wording: Secure intravenous access if the placenta is retained, and explain to the woman why this is needed.

pass: IV access is documented as secured at the time retained placenta is diagnosed, with a note that the reason was explained to the woman
population: Inclusion: all women with a placenta not delivered within 30 minutes (active management) or 60 minutes (physiological management) of birth. Exclusion: women who already had IV access in place for another reason before diagnosis (record as already in place).
sample: 20-30 consecutive women with a retained placenta over the last 6-12 months
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'retained placenta' sticker/proforma triggered at 30 or 60 minutes (as applicable) on the third-stage record, with a mandatory IV access field.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward audit meeting; if compliant, embed the proforma in standard third-stage documentation
evidence: no closed-loop audit of IV access for retained placenta found in the library
pitfalls: Retained placenta is relatively infrequent → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
IV access may be secured but not documented as related to the retained placenta specifically → check the timing against the diagnosis time
Community/home births have different equipment and transfer implications → consider auditing hospital and home births separately
Explanation to the woman is often given verbally without being noted → add a simple documentation prompt
Fading compliance without an automatic prompt → build the 30/60-minute retained placenta alert into the electronic partogram
pearls: Involve the labour ward coordinator in designing the retained placenta proforma
Use simulation training on postpartum haemorrhage and retained placenta to reinforce the IV access step
Track subsequent haemorrhage rate as a linked outcome measure
Coordinate with the community/home birth team on transfer protocols for this scenario
Keep the same 30/60-minute definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per case from the birth record

question: Of women having outpatient induction of labour, what proportion had a full clinical assessment of the woman and baby, and an agreed review plan, documented before they were discharged home?
why: Outpatient induction relies on safe assessment and a clear review plan before the woman leaves the unit; no closed-loop audit of pre-discharge assessment completeness for outpatient induction is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG207 Inducing labour, rec 1.6.2 and rec 1.6.3 (2008, amended 2021)
standard.wording: Carry out a full clinical assessment of the woman and baby (see recommendations 1.5.1 and 1.5.2) and ensure safety and support procedures are in place. ... For induction being undertaken on an outpatient basis, agree a review plan with the woman before she returns home.

pass: A full clinical assessment (Bishop score, CTG) and an agreed, documented review plan (including when to return, or when to contact the unit) are both recorded before the woman is discharged home
population: Inclusion: all women having outpatient induction of labour. Exclusion: women converted to inpatient induction before any planned discharge home.
sample: 30 consecutive outpatient inductions over the last 3-6 months
data_source: Induction of labour outpatient pathway record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a structured outpatient induction discharge checklist with mandatory assessment and review-plan fields that must be completed before the woman can be marked as discharged home.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the induction of labour/maternity governance meeting; if compliant, make the checklist the standard outpatient induction discharge document
evidence: no closed-loop audit of pre-discharge assessment completeness for outpatient induction found in the library
pitfalls: Outpatient induction volumes may be modest → extend the collection period to 3-6 months
Review plan sometimes given verbally without being written down → require a written plan given to the woman as well as documented in the notes
Safety-netting advice content varies between staff → use a standard script or leaflet for consistency
Unplanned reattendance before the planned review may indicate inadequate initial safety-netting → track and review these cases
Fading compliance without a mandatory checklist → build the checklist into the EPR discharge workflow
pearls: Involve the outpatient induction pathway lead midwife as co-investigator
Provide a standard written safety-netting leaflet for all outpatient induction patients
Track unplanned reattendance rate as a linked safety outcome measure
Share learning from any adverse outcome after outpatient induction at the governance meeting
Keep the same assessment and review-plan definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the outpatient induction record

question: Of women who gave birth following spontaneous preterm labour before 34 weeks' gestation, what proportion received intravenous intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis against early-onset group B streptococcal infection?
why: Preterm birth carries a substantially higher risk of early-onset GBS infection regardless of known maternal GBS status, and this preterm-specific antibiotic standard is distinct from the existing audit of antibiotics for women with a known GBS-positive result at term [NNA-200]; no audit of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for preterm labour under 34 weeks is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 5, process indicator 5d (2023)
standard.wording: Percentage of women who give birth following preterm labour below 34 weeks of gestation who receive IV intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent early onset neonatal Group B Streptococcal (GBS) infection.

pass: IV intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis against GBS is given during labour to a woman giving birth following spontaneous preterm labour before 34 weeks
population: Inclusion: women giving birth following spontaneous preterm labour before 34+0 weeks. Exclusion: elective preterm birth for a maternal or fetal indication with no labour, women with a documented penicillin/antibiotic contraindication managed with an alternative agent (record as compliant with an alternative).
sample: 20-30 consecutive preterm births below 34 weeks following spontaneous labour over the last 6-12 months
data_source: Labour ward drug chart and birth record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'preterm labour under 34 weeks' order set to e-prescribing that defaults to IV benzylpenicillin (or the locally agreed alternative) regardless of known GBS status, triggered when gestation under 34 weeks is entered.
reaudit: At 6-12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the preterm birth/perinatal optimisation pathway meeting; if compliant, report through the SBLCB v3 element 5 process indicators
evidence: [NNA-200] audits intrapartum antibiotics for known GBS-positive status at term; this audit covers preterm labour under 34 weeks regardless of GBS status, not previously audited in the library
pitfalls: Very preterm births are infrequent per unit → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
Staff may only think to give antibiotics if GBS status is known positive, missing the preterm-specific indication → make the order set trigger on gestation alone, not GBS status
Rapid/precipitate preterm births may not allow time for antibiotics before birth → record time from labour onset (or arrival) to first dose to distinguish this from omission
This is a distinct standard from the term GBS-positive antibiotic audit already in the library → keep the two audits and their process indicators clearly separate in reporting
Fading compliance without an order-set default → embed the trigger by gestation in the electronic prescribing system
pearls: Cross-reference with the existing term GBS antibiotic audit [NNA-200] but report separately to avoid confusion
Involve the preterm birth team and labour ward pharmacist in building the order set
Track early-onset neonatal GBS infection rates in preterm babies as a linked outcome measure
Report through the perinatal optimisation pathway compliance metric alongside the other SBLCB v3 element 5 measures
Keep the same 34-week gestation cut-off at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per case from the drug chart and birth record

question: What proportion of parents were given information, before discharge, on the 'red flag' signs of serious illness in young babies that should prompt an urgent or emergency review?
why: Delayed recognition of serious neonatal illness after discharge is a recurring theme in serious incident reviews; no closed-loop audit of red-flag safety-netting information given at discharge is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG194 Postnatal care, rec 1.4.9 and rec 1.4.10 (2021)
standard.wording: Recognise the following as 'red flags' for serious illness in young babies: appearing ill to a healthcare professional, appearing pale, ashen, mottled or blue (cyanosis), unresponsive or unrousable ... If a baby is thought to be seriously unwell based on a 'red flag' ... or on an overall assessment of their condition, arrange an immediate assessment with an appropriate emergency service.

pass: The discharge record documents that parents were given verbal and/or written information on newborn red-flag symptoms and when to seek urgent or emergency help
population: Inclusion: all babies discharged home from the birth setting or postnatal ward. Exclusion: babies transferred directly to another hospital or the neonatal unit.
sample: 40 consecutive babies discharged home over the last 4-6 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a standard newborn red-flag safety-netting leaflet to the discharge pack, with a mandatory 'red flag information given' tick box on the electronic discharge checklist.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the postnatal ward/neonatal governance meeting; if compliant, extend the leaflet to home birth discharge packs
evidence: no closed-loop audit of newborn red-flag safety-netting information at discharge found in the library
pitfalls: Verbal-only advice is easily forgotten by tired new parents → always pair verbal advice with a written leaflet
Documentation of 'advice given' is often generic and does not specify red flags → require the specific red-flag leaflet to be named in the record
Parents with limited English or literacy needs may need alternative formats → ensure translated or accessible versions are available and their use recorded
Fading compliance without a mandatory field → build the tick box into the electronic discharge checklist
Different discharge pathways (early transfer, home birth) may be missed by a single checklist → apply the same check to all discharge routes
pearls: Base the leaflet directly on the NG194 red-flag list for consistency with national guidance
Involve neonatal outreach/community midwifery teams in leaflet design and distribution
Audit understanding, not just receipt, with a brief follow-up question at the next contact if feasible
Share any serious incident learning (anonymised) to reinforce staff engagement
Keep the same red-flag list and format categories at re-audit
effort: ~10 min per 10 discharges from the discharge checklist

question: What proportion of women had a documented postnatal reassessment of their venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk before discharge from postnatal care?
why: VTE risk changes after birth and a postnatal reassessment determines the need for continued thromboprophylaxis; this is distinct from the booking risk assessment already audited above, and no closed-loop audit of postnatal VTE reassessment is in the library.

standard.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37a, Reducing the Risk of Venous Thromboembolism during Pregnancy and the Puerperium (April 2015, amended 2023)
standard.wording: usually require prophylactic LMWH for 6 weeks postnatally but a postnatal risk reassessment should be made.

pass: A documented VTE risk reassessment is recorded before discharge from postnatal inpatient care, with a clear plan for continued or stopped thromboprophylaxis
population: Inclusion: all women being discharged from postnatal inpatient care. Exclusion: women who did not have any antenatal risk factors for VTE and had a straightforward vaginal birth with no intrapartum risk factors (very low risk, reassessment still recommended but often brief).
sample: 40 consecutive women discharged from postnatal inpatient care over the last 4-6 weeks
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory postnatal VTE risk reassessment field to the electronic discharge checklist, pre-populated with the antenatal risk factors for review and updating with any new intrapartum risk factors (for example, caesarean birth, prolonged labour, haemorrhage).
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity thrombosis committee; if compliant, extend the mandatory field to postnatal readmissions
evidence: no closed-loop audit of postnatal VTE risk reassessment before discharge found in the library
pitfalls: Reassessment may be assumed rather than actively documented if the booking assessment was normal → require an explicit postnatal entry, not just reference to the booking assessment
Caesarean births automatically carry additional risk factors that must be captured → ensure the reassessment tool includes intrapartum and mode-of-birth factors
Early discharge (within 24 hours) can compress the time available for reassessment → include timing of reassessment relative to discharge in the data
Duplication with the booking VTE audit above may confuse staff → make clear in training that this is a separate, postnatal check
Fading compliance without a mandatory field → build the postnatal reassessment into the EPR discharge workflow
pearls: Pair this audit with the booking VTE risk assessment audit above to give a complete picture of the pathway
Involve the maternity thrombosis lead midwife/obstetrician as co-investigator
Cross-check a sample of women given continued LMWH to confirm the correct duration was prescribed and supplied at discharge
Present alongside MBRRACE-UK data on VTE as a leading cause of direct maternal death
Keep the same reassessment definition and mode-of-birth categories at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the discharge checklist
